newsitem.title: USA: FDA clears breakthrough device to control shakes.
newsitem.headline: FDA clears breakthrough device to control shakes.

text.p: Maurice Long, who shakes visibly due to a neurological disorder, has no trouble getting wagers on the golf course.

At the first tee, his trembling convinces other players he can be easily beaten, but he has a trick. Implanted in his chest near his collarbone is a breakthrough electronic device that controls the shakes.
Once the bets are in and tee off time arrives, Long switches the device back on and plays a solid and tremor-free game, often leaving his companions in the rough.
"It only works once with each foursome," said the 72-year-old retired farmer from Hutchinson, Kansas.

The device in Long's chest is the Activa system, which was approved Monday for marketing by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as the first all-new therapy to hit the market in 30 years for controlling what is called "essential tremor."
Minneapolis-based Medtronic Inc., maker of the $9,500-per-unit Activa, said it expects about 100,000 Americans may be candidates to receive it.

Essential tremor is the most common neurological movement disorder in the country and affects at least a million Americans, usually age 45 and older. Tremor is also a major symptom of Parkinson's Disease, which affects about 500,000 Americans.

"I inherited it from my mother. It runs in the family ... For me, it got to the point where I couldn't eat. I couldn't write my name. I hated to go out in public. It was not life-threatening, but it was very debilitating," he said.
After 14 years of largely ineffective drug treatment and gradually worsening shakes, Long sought help from Dr. William Koller at University of Kansas Medical Centre.

"The Activa system is a safe and adaptable therapy for patients whose drug therapy has been ineffective," said Dr. Koller, chairman of the university medical center's neurology department in Kansas City, Kan.

In an operation last year, the matchbox-sized Activa electronic pulse generator -- similar to a pacemaker -- was placed in Long's chest. A wire was threaded up his neck and deep into the thalamus area of his brain.
By sending mild electrical shocks to the thalamus, the system blocks the brain signals that caused his tremors.

"They gave me surgery one day and I was home the next day and out on the putting green....It's an immediate thing. As soon as you wake up from surgery, you have more control than you've had for years," Long said.
Medicare and private insurer reimbursement for the Activa is available in most states, Medtronic said.
The patient controls the system by passing a hand-held magnet over the skin near the generator to turn it off and on, as needed to control symptoms.
Long said he switches his Activa off at bedtime and back on in the morning, which prolongs the three-to-five year life of the battery.
"It's a miracle. That's the only thing I can say. I can do anything I want to do now," he said, adding he has had only one negative side-effect from the implant.
"My wife is making me do more household chores than she used to. So that's the downside," he said.
